title: Structured validation of syndromic surveillance alerts in a regional public health agency
subtitle: Design not yet settled: accuracy study or randomised comparison of validation procedures
statement: About 35 syndromic surveillance alerts a week are validated by the epidemiologist on duty without a written procedure, with large differences in time spent and at least one recent cluster dismissed twice before escalation. A structured checklist has been drafted. Whether to evaluate it as a test (accuracy against a reference) or as a change in procedure (effect on time to decision and on missed events) is not yet settled, and the choice determines what the director will learn.
whoAffected: Residents of the region, especially people in care homes and small rural communities where outbreaks are detected through few cases; the six duty epidemiologists; local health units that act on escalations.
whatHurts: A real outbreak dismissed as an artefact delays control measures, as in the care home norovirus cluster last winter; hours spent on false alerts take epidemiologists away from other work.
currentPractice: Unwritten validation by the epidemiologist on duty, ranging from minutes to hours per alert; no measurement of dismissed true events.
whyNow: A drafted checklist, a director who wants evidence before making it standard, and a six-month evaluation window from January 2027.
constraints: No new staff; six epidemiologists on the duty rota; a six-month evaluation from January to June 2027; alert logs and later outbreak reports are the only data sources.
patientCenteredGoal: Real outbreaks, including small ones in care homes and rural areas, are recognised on the first alert, and staff time goes where it protects people.
summary: Problem framed; the design family is left unresolved between an accuracy study and a randomised comparison.
